stimulus.title: Opening Remarks: The Elmwood Community Observatory
stimulus.body: Students, parents and neighbours, welcome to the opening night of our community observatory. Five years ago, this hilltop held nothing more than a disused water tank and a patch of kikuyu grass. Today, thanks to local bricklayers, retired engineers, and Year 6 students who sold hundreds of trays of seedlings, a rotating dome stands ready to welcome every curious mind in our postcode. Some asked why a suburban school should invest in a telescope when dazzling images from space probes are freely available online. My answer is simple: seeing Saturn's rings on a screen is impressive, but seeing that pale golden ring-system live through an eyepiece—knowing that the light striking your eye left Saturn more than an hour ago—changes how you feel about your place in the universe. Tonight, as the dome opens to the southern sky, I invite every student here to ask a question that has no easy answer.

stimulus.title: Bringing Back the Billabong: Restoring the Murray Wetlands
stimulus.body: For decades, engineers treated river floodplains mainly as channels to move irrigation water quickly downstream. Levee banks kept seasonal floods off low-lying paddocks, unintentionally starving hundreds of billabongs and river red gum forests of the periodic soaking they evolved to depend on. Over the past ten years, however, ecologists and local landholders along the Murray River have tested a quieter partnership. By installing small, adjustable regulator gates in old earthen banks, environmental water managers can mimic natural spring floods, guiding water into dried-out wetlands for a few weeks before letting it drain slowly back to the main river. The response has been swift. Within months of a single managed watering, dormant frog species emerge from cracked clay, waterbirds return to nest in inundated lignum bushes, and young native fish shelter in the warm, food-rich backwaters before rejoining the main channel.
